questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: As my exchange was in spring 2023, I had to apply already in October 2021 where COVID-19 was still very much on everybody's mind, so although it's quite boring reason to choose your study destination I wanted to choose a country that I hoped would deal with a new wave/break out of covid well including having a decent health care system. Other factors that were important to me were that I could speak the language kind of coherently and that I hadn't visited the country before.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall, I had a good experience, and I'm really happy that I went, because I had a few personal issues to work out. However, I started classes on January 7th, and was finished with exams and everything April 15th which means I only had school for three months and a week which, to me, was timeframe I would have wished was longer, as I hadn't properly settled in and made friends until around the two month mark (leaving not that long to fully enjoy that studying abroad life). I'm a bit introverted though, so might not be a problem if you're more extroverted / quicker at making friends :) The upside of this short term is that I had an amazing long summer break to go explore the remaining parts of Toronto and Canada :)

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Most information was sent to me through the UofT email system, and I highly recommend reading them and reading them THOUROUGHLY. The UofT inbound site was also so so helpful. Generally speaking, you're kind on your own in figuring everything out :)

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
After the first week of class there was a meeting for inbound (and outbound?) exchange students. The meeting mostly focused on stuff that I was already aware of such as the mandatory healthcare plan (what it covers, how it's paid) and telling students to make sure that they're getting the right credits to be able to
graduate....so
like very practical / technical stuff and not anything about how to adjust to UofT as an academic institution.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I wish it had been maybe the day before classes started, and maybe could also have included a tour of campus or like some info on how to get help for papers and stuff (like information about the amazing writing centers) or anything that has an impact on day to day living as a student.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Already applying to UofT they make clear that they DO NOT help with finding housing. I definitely underestimated how stressfull finding housing would be. UofT housing services did have a great zoom meeting on how to find off-campus housing and what to be aware of in regards to tenants right and so on that was extremely helpful! I used the official UofT "roommate finder" tool/website, and did end up talking to a girl who needed a roommate for the semester, but ultimately ended up at Tartu College (off campus dorms) because it was a bit cheaper and with an actual contract :)

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Renting by yourself is HARD if you're only staying for one semester. Most landlords only offer 12 month contracts (including UofT's own on campus residences) and subletting the first/last six months can be a difficult and complicated proces. Most landlords also demand a guarantor and canadian bank account.  All the exchange students I met who had rented an apartment or room in an apartment regretted it doing it. I recommend looking into Tartu College! The dorms are very cheap (compared to Toronto prices) and it's across the street from campus, so despite living off-campus you basically ARE living on campus. It's also very professionally run with a 24 hour service desk and pretty easy to apply to.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did apply to UofT's own residences, but lots of them only have 12 month contract and you're only guaranteed a spot in one of the dorms if you're a freshman/1st year. I was offered a spot after signing my contract with Tartu, but that was like 2 weeks before the term started.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I found it pretty easy, definitely a plus that all parts of the process can be done online! Easy process, but a bit tiresome / long with lots of steps to it.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
After receiving a spot through the KU exchange program, I received a mail to UofT's inbound application website where I had to go through most of the steps of the KU application again (which classes do you expect to be taking, personal information and so on). When UofT then approved my application, I had to convert my application login to a UofT student login and login to all their portals and email system. Then I had to apply to classes through a google forms. The form itself was easy to fill out and the explaining email on how to do it was pretty detailed, but figuring out was classes I could apply to (most have prerequisites) and ensuring that they don't overlap took a long, long
time...like
i spend maybe a week figuring it out. Lastly I had to apply for the health insurance, and then I think I was good to go :)

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Emails being sent to my UofT email, and then sending emails with questions if I had any.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: A lot of the classes I originally wanted, I couldn't take because of prerequisites, but all the classes I applied to I got into :) But I also applied in application round 2 I think? There are 5 total as far as I remember, so being quick can definitely be smart, because popular classes fill up pretty fast! (This meant I applied for classes in July/August 2022 even though my stay didn't start till January)

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Learn what the different aspects of the course codes means quickly, and take your time looking through the course catalogue. And check your emails. Seriously. Each course application round only had a week to do it in, so it's pretty easy to miss a round if you aren't checking your UofT email frequently :)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I think it depends a lot on your classes, as the content of the class and what makes up your final grade is very much up to the professor teaching. As a humanities student I had to write and turn in A LOT of smaller papers (compared to KU). Across four classes I had 13 papers/essays varying from being 2-4 pages to 10-15 pages in three months. That was a lot for me personally, as the reading amount was still similar or more than what I'm used to from KU. UofT definitely has a hustle culture and there's always lots of people in the library even on the weekends or if it's 10 pm/22:00 :)

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had two 200 level courses and two 300 level courses (two rhetoric courses, two literature). I don't think the work level / expectations to students differed from 200 level courses and 300 level courses, but was more up to the professor of the course. Like my 200 level 'Introduction to Canadian Literature' was probably the one with the lowest expectations in regards to how well thought out your essays had to be, whereas my rhetoric course on that level had bigger requirements :) But seriously, try to put some 'easy' courses in there! If all the courses are going to be challenging for you, your workload could be A LOT if you want to do well.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Varied from class to class. From KU I'm used to classes with 30-60 people in them with part lecture/part group work and discussion (always a practical element). At UofT I had classes like that, but also classes that were only discussions or only lectures.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
ENG252H1-S (Introduction to Canadian Literature)
WGS380H1-S (Feminist Graphic Novels)
WRR201H1-S (Theories of Rhetoric: A History of Persuasion)
WRR3081H-S (Selected Topics in Writing and Rhetoric: Visual Rhetoric)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
My favorite courses were (surprisingly?) the ones that weren't rhetoric! 
Feminist Graphic Novels was an AMAZING course, and ended up being my favorite despite having chosen it as my "lol course". The class is super intersectional, and covers a wide range of topics, the text selection is phenomenal, and there's a fine line between 'academic observations' and personal experiences in the class discussions. Highly recommend! 
Intro. to Canadian Lit. is a great class for learning a bit about Canadian culture and history from a different angle! Each week was basically a different period in literature with a text from that time period, and the lecture would offer lots of cultural and historical context for help unpacking, starting from First Nations voices and settlement narratives to modern day criticisms on Canada's multiculturalism policy from minorities :) I was pretty nervous as I didn't know anything about Canada, but if you just turn up to the lectures and listen (and read), it will be pretty easy to pass :)

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Groceries were definitely a lot more expensive than expected...vegetables were a lot more expensive than in Denmark :) I did a lot of personal spending because I wanted to be able to go out and experience the things I wanted to do.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries were more than expected. Going out is same prices as in Denmark when you add 13% tax + 15-20% tip to the price :)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There were lots of opportunities! Great fitness facilities to drop into, clubs to join that had ski trips and so on. Visit the harthouse website!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Honestly a lot! Workout classes, fitness center, great student theatre productions, clubs and so on. The harthouse website has them on there, you just need to know it exists!

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I went to the theatre productions / festival (very high level student productions) and a few of the exchange student events.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Kensington Market is so cute -- also has a very fun (and professional) open mic night on tuesdays at Supermarket Bar. Toronto Islands is great and cute if the weather is nice! And ofc. you need to watch Ice Hockey! In general, just go and explore the city :) And spend money on all the amazing food you can't get at home like soup dumplings, Caribien, actually authentic Mexican (Taco Gus at Kensington) and much more. For every country's cuisine there's a restaurant. But like obvious stuff like ice skating and Niagara Falls. Taking the train to Montreal or Quebec is also a great way to spent reading week.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy, no big culture shock. (I have lived in the US before though, so you might have a different experience). The biggest difference is definitely that Toronto is extremely multicultural compared to Copenhagen (which I loved), and VERY queer friendly (yes, way more than Copenhagen).

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just talk! They're pretty nice so just go ahead! And like get their Instagrams and/or phone numbers and stuff. But yeah, sit down and chat with the person next to you in class.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Mostly just figuring out what the expectations / genre conventions of "the undergraduate academic essay" were and like what was expected academically. Night life is also a bit different, as the clubs close at 2 (yes), and are pretty dead if it isn't Friday or Saturday, and you aren't allowed (in Ontario) to walk around with alcohol in public, but weed is legal and very much allowed (and smelt)
everywhere...but
nothing actually challenging :)

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The stereotype of Canadians being very nice and helpful IS true, and it feels much more authentic than in the US. Over 51% of people living in Toronto are born outside Canada, so Toronto is incredibly multicultural which is very fun to experience (and makes for great food experiences), but it's definitely also a 'hustle city'. Toronto is also the most queerfriendly place I've ever visited/been which is awesome! Church Street has some great queer clubs and events to go to, and queer PDA is frequently seen everywhere in the city.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Don't get too caught up in UofT's hustle
culture...you
don't need to do all the readings or write the most amazing essay, you just need to pass. Explore the city.
2. Do your research in regards to practical aspects such as courses to take, how to sign up for things and so on. You're on your own kid.
3. I really recommend looking into Tartu College, and seeing if that could be good housing choice for you. Easy and professional process (but consider paying for a room with aircon if you're there in the summer, it supposedly gets next level hot)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be aware that you might have to sign up for courses more than six months in advance!! check your email!!!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Leaning into the 'big city lifestyle'. It sounds dumb but walking around Toronto with iced coffee from Tim Hortons made me feel like 'that girl', and I really recommend leaning into all the unique experiences that living in a city of that size can bring (like there being great concerts, a drag scene, amazing restaurants and so on). And making connections and friends of course.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Making friends, hahah. Not that it was that hard, but I definitely felt lonely and overwhelmed for the first month and a half, but I also turned in my bachelor assignment three minutes before the deadline a day before my flight to Canada,  so I just hadn't had a lot of time to process / had had a few stressful months before my stay which did impact my first time in Toronto.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Toronto is an amazing city! The neighborhoods vary so much, which means that the city has a lot of different vibes to offer depending in where you're walking around. And please, if you end up at UofT EXPLORE the libraries and don't just go to Robarts - there are so many cute small and Harry Potter-esque libraries if you explore a bit (Emmanual College is a good place to start).

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
